questions.stem: In psychology, personality refers to a person's:
options: level of intellectual ability compared with others their age
temporary mood on a particular day or in one situation
physical appearance and the way they present themselves
characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving
questions.explanation: Personality is the set of relatively stable, characteristic patterns of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that make each person distinctive. Moods are temporary, and intelligence is a separate individual difference.

questions.stem: Twin studies find that identical twins are more alike in personality traits than fraternal twins, even when raised apart. This is evidence that personality:
options: is shaped by the shared family home
is fixed by birth order
is partly heritable
is entirely learned
questions.explanation: Greater similarity in identical twins, who share all their genes, points to a genetic contribution. Twin studies also show substantial environmental influence, so personality is not entirely inherited.

questions.stem: A report says a personality trait has a heritability of about 0.5. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The trait will be passed from parent to child in about half of all families
About half the variation in that population relates to genetic differences
Half of each person's level of the trait was inherited and half was learned
Half of all people inherit the trait and the other half learn it from parents
questions.explanation: Heritability is a population statistic: the share of variation between people that is associated with genetic variation. It does not split one individual's trait into inherited and learned parts.

questions.stem: A projective test of personality, such as the Rorschach inkblot test, works by:
options: timing responses to simple visual stimuli
asking people to interpret ambiguous images
asking people to rate statements about themselves
observing behaviour in a range of real situations
questions.explanation: Projective tests present ambiguous stimuli, such as inkblots or unclear pictures, on the assumption that people project unconscious thoughts and feelings into their interpretations.

questions.stem: In the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), a person is shown ambiguous pictures of people and asked to:
options: say what shape they see in each symmetrical inkblot
rate how much they agree with each statement shown
tell a story about what is happening in each picture
choose which of two statements best describes them
questions.explanation: The TAT asks people to make up a story about each picture, including what led up to the scene and how it ends. The themes are interpreted as revealing their needs and motives.

questions.stem: Two psychologists score the same person's Rorschach responses and reach different conclusions. Which weakness of projective tests does this show?
options: cultural bias, because the inkblots are all the same
the placebo effect, because the person expected a result
low inter-rater reliability, because scoring is subjective
low external validity, because the sample was too small
questions.explanation: Projective test responses must be interpreted by the scorer, and different scorers can disagree. Low inter-rater reliability also undermines the test's validity.

questions.stem: The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is based on the ideas of:
options: Sigmund Freud
Hans Eysenck
B. F. Skinner
Carl Jung
questions.explanation: The MBTI was developed by Katharine Briggs and Isabel Briggs Myers from Jung's theory of psychological types, including introversion and extraversion.

questions.stem: The MBTI sorts people into one of how many personality types?
questions.explanation: The MBTI combines four pairs of preferences (extraversion or introversion, sensing or intuition, thinking or feeling, judging or perceiving), giving 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 types.

questions.stem: A company uses the MBTI to decide which applicants to hire. Which is the strongest criticism of this practice?
options: The MBTI measures intelligence, so it cannot be used to assess personality
The MBTI uses inkblots, so the scoring of each applicant is too subjective
The MBTI gives a score on only one trait, so it is too narrow to be useful
Many people get a different type on retest, so it is unreliable
questions.explanation: Research shows many people receive a different type when retested weeks later, and sorting people into either-or types ignores that most score near the middle. Its predictive validity for job performance is weak.

questions.stem: Personality inventories such as the NEO-PI are used in workplace selection. Which is a limitation of these self-report inventories?
options: They rely on interpreting ambiguous images and stories
They give results that cannot be compared with norms
Applicants may answer in ways that make them look good
They can only be scored by a trained psychoanalyst
questions.explanation: Self-report inventories are open to social desirability bias, especially when a job depends on the answers. They are standardised and objectively scored, unlike projective tests.

questions.stem: In Freud's theory, which part of the personality acts as the conscience?
options: the superego
the id
the ego
the libido
questions.explanation: The superego holds internalised moral standards and produces guilt. The id seeks immediate pleasure, and the ego balances the two against reality.

questions.stem: In Freud's theory, the ego operates on:
options: the reality principle
the pleasure principle
the morality principle
the inferiority principle
questions.explanation: The ego works on the reality principle, finding realistic ways to satisfy the id's demands within the limits of the real world and the superego.

questions.stem: A student who is angry with his teacher shouts at his younger brother when he gets home. Which Freudian defence mechanism is this?
options: projection
sublimation
displacement
repression
questions.explanation: Displacement redirects feelings from a threatening target to a safer one. Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of Freud's psychosexual stages?
options: oral, phallic, anal, latency, genital
oral, anal, latency, phallic, genital
oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital
anal, oral, phallic, genital, latency
questions.explanation: Freud proposed the oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital stages. He argued that conflicts unresolved at a stage can lead to fixation that shows in adult personality.

questions.stem: How did Jung's view of the unconscious differ from Freud's?
options: Jung believed the unconscious could be measured by reaction times
Jung added a collective unconscious of archetypes shared by all
Jung argued there was no unconscious mind and studied only behaviour
Jung saw the unconscious as made only of repressed childhood wishes
questions.explanation: Jung accepted a personal unconscious but added the collective unconscious, inherited and shared by all people, containing archetypes such as the persona and the shadow.

questions.stem: Which is the main scientific criticism of psychodynamic theories?
options: They explain personality only in terms of reinforcement and rewards
Key ideas, such as unconscious conflict, are hard to test or falsify
They ignore childhood experiences and focus only on adult behaviour
They are based on large controlled experiments with random samples
questions.explanation: Concepts like the id or the collective unconscious cannot be directly observed or measured, so the theories are difficult to test. Freud's evidence came mainly from case studies of his own patients.

questions.stem: Humanist theories of personality emphasise:
options: learned responses to rewards and punishments
a small number of inherited, stable traits
free will, conscious choices and personal growth
unconscious drives and early childhood conflicts
questions.explanation: Humanists such as Rogers and Maslow focus on each person's conscious experience, free will and drive towards growth and self-actualisation.

questions.stem: According to Rogers, a person experiences incongruence when:
options: their self-concept differs greatly from their experience
their basic needs for food and safety are not being met
their id and superego come into conflict with each other
their behaviour is punished more often than it is rewarded
questions.explanation: Rogers argued that a large gap between self-concept (including the ideal self) and actual experience produces incongruence and anxiety. Congruence supports healthy functioning.

questions.stem: Parents who love and accept their child even when the child misbehaves, while disapproving of the behaviour, are showing what Rogers called:
options: conditions of worth
continuous positive reinforcement
reciprocal determinism
unconditional positive regard
questions.explanation: Unconditional positive regard is acceptance of a person regardless of their behaviour. Conditions of worth arise when love is given only when the child meets certain standards.

questions.stem: According to Maslow, why might a student who is often unsafe at home not work towards self-actualisation?
options: Self-actualisation is reached only by people who are hungry and unsafe
Safety needs sit at the top of the hierarchy and are met last of all
Unsafe environments reinforce the student for avoiding personal growth
Lower needs such as safety must be largely met before higher ones
questions.explanation: Maslow proposed a hierarchy in which physiological and safety needs must be reasonably satisfied before belonging, esteem and self-actualisation needs become the main motivators.

questions.stem: Which is a common criticism of humanist theories of personality?
options: Concepts such as self-actualisation are vague and hard to measure
They treat people as passive and controlled by their environment
They are based mainly on experiments with rats and pigeons
They focus too much on unconscious sexual and aggressive drives
questions.explanation: Ideas like self-actualisation and congruence are difficult to define and test objectively. Seeing people as passive products of the environment is a criticism of behaviourism, not humanism.

questions.stem: From Skinner's behaviourist view, a child who is consistently praised for being helpful develops a 'helpful personality' because:
options: a helpful trait was inherited at birth
the child's superego has become very strong
the child is moving towards self-actualisation
the helpful behaviour has been reinforced
questions.explanation: Skinner saw personality as a set of learned behaviours shaped by their consequences. Behaviours that are reinforced become more frequent and form the patterns others call personality.

questions.stem: Which is a key criticism of the behaviourist approach to personality?
options: It assumes all people strive for growth and self-actualisation
It explains personality using archetypes shared by all humans
It ignores thoughts, feelings and inherited differences
It relies on projective tests that have low inter-rater reliability
questions.explanation: By focusing only on observable behaviour and the environment, behaviourism largely ignores cognition, emotion and genetic influences. Social cognitive theorists added cognitive factors to address this.

questions.stem: Bandura's idea of reciprocal determinism proposes that personality arises from interactions between:
options: the id, the ego and the superego
the conscious, personal and collective unconscious
physiological, safety and esteem needs
the person, their behaviour and the environment
questions.explanation: Bandura argued that personal factors (such as thoughts and self-efficacy), behaviour and the environment all influence each other. People are shaped by their environment but also shape it.

questions.stem: A student believes she can succeed in maths if she practises, so she keeps trying difficult problems. In Bandura's theory, this belief is called:
options: self-efficacy
self-actualisation
a condition of worth
an archetype
questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is a person's belief in their ability to succeed at a particular task. High self-efficacy leads people to attempt challenges and persist.

questions.stem: A student believes his exam results depend mainly on luck and the difficulty of the paper. In Rotter's terms, he has:
options: a strong superego
an external locus of control
an internal locus of control
high self-efficacy
questions.explanation: Rotter's locus of control describes where people believe control over outcomes lies. Believing results depend on luck or others reflects an external locus of control.

questions.stem: A boy is talkative and confident with friends but quiet and anxious in class. How would Mischel explain this?
options: Behaviour depends on the person interacting with the situation
His traits are fixed, so one of the observations must be wrong
His superego is stronger at school than it is with his friends
He has not yet satisfied his needs for belonging and esteem
questions.explanation: Mischel argued that behaviour is not consistent across situations as trait theories assume. A person's behaviour reflects how they interpret and respond to each specific situation.

questions.stem: Mischel's criticism of trait theories was that:
options: traits are inherited, so personality tests cannot measure them reliably
traits explain only unconscious conflicts rather than everyday behaviour
traits apply only to people who have reached self-actualisation
traits often predict poorly how a person behaves across situations
questions.explanation: Mischel found that people's behaviour in one situation often correlated only weakly with their behaviour in another, so broad traits predicted specific behaviour poorly. This began the person-situation debate.

questions.stem: Trait theories of personality aim to:
options: explain personality only as the result of past reinforcements
describe and measure lasting characteristics of people
explain how unconscious conflicts in childhood shape adult behaviour
show how people move towards self-actualisation over their lifetime
questions.explanation: Trait theorists identify and measure stable characteristics, such as extraversion, on which people differ. They focus on describing personality rather than explaining how it develops.

questions.stem: Allport described a trait so dominant that it shapes almost everything a person does, such as extreme ambition, as a:
options: source trait
cardinal trait
central trait
secondary trait
questions.explanation: Allport proposed cardinal traits (dominating a whole life, found in few people), central traits (the main building blocks of personality) and secondary traits (preferences shown only in some situations).

questions.stem: Cattell used factor analysis to identify how many source traits in his personality model?
questions.explanation: Cattell reduced a large list of trait words to 16 source traits, measured by his 16 Personality Factor (16PF) questionnaire. Eysenck proposed three dimensions and the five-factor model five.

questions.stem: Eysenck's PEN model describes personality using which three dimensions?
options: psychoticism, extraversion, neuroticism
openness, extraversion, neuroticism
persona, ego, neuroticism
perception, emotion, needs
questions.explanation: PEN stands for psychoticism, extraversion and neuroticism. Eysenck first proposed extraversion and neuroticism and later added psychoticism.

questions.stem: Eysenck proposed a biological basis for extraversion. According to his theory, introverts:
options: have higher baseline cortical arousal, so avoid extra stimulation
have lower baseline cortical arousal, so they seek out stimulation
have a stronger superego, which makes them quieter in social settings
have been punished more often for talking than extraverts have been
questions.explanation: Eysenck argued introverts have a naturally higher level of cortical arousal and so prefer quieter settings, while extraverts have lower arousal and seek stimulation to raise it.

questions.stem: Which list gives the five factors in Costa and McCrae's five-factor model?
options: optimism, conscientiousness, empathy, agreeableness, nervousness
openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, assertiveness, narcissism
openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
openness, confidence, extraversion, ambition, neuroticism
questions.explanation: The five factors, often remembered as OCEAN, are openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. They are measured by the NEO-PI.

questions.stem: A worker is organised, reliable and always meets deadlines. On the five-factor model she would score high on:
options: openness
extraversion
conscientiousness
agreeableness
questions.explanation: Conscientiousness describes being organised, dependable, disciplined and achievement-focused. Agreeableness relates to being cooperative and kind.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares trait theories with humanist theories?
options: Trait theories focus on unconscious drives; humanist theories focus on reinforcement
Both rely mainly on projective tests to assess unconscious parts of the personality
Both argue that behaviour is controlled entirely by the external environment
Trait theories measure differences; humanist theories focus on growth and the self
questions.explanation: Trait theories measure stable characteristics using questionnaires and statistics. Humanist theories focus on subjective experience, the self and the drive to self-actualise.

questions.stem: The interactionist view of personality holds that:
options: personality is fixed by genes and not affected by experience at all
personality is learned entirely from the rewards a person receives
personality depends only on the stage at which a person is fixated
inherited temperament and experience combine to shape personality
questions.explanation: Twin and adoption studies show that both genes and environment matter, and they influence each other. For example, an inherited temperament affects how others respond to a child.
